title: Data center capacity for neoclouds and AI labs: power, space and cooling for your GPUs (2026)
description: Where neoclouds and smaller AI labs find data center capacity in 2026: MW per GPU count, colocation vs powered shell vs land, liquid cooling, and how to check a power date.
intro: Neoclouds and smaller AI labs find capacity in three places: colocation halls that can take dense liquid-cooled racks, built or energized sites they can lease whole, and powered land they build on. The right one depends on cluster size and how soon you need it. A 1,024-GPU B200 cluster draws about 2.6 MW at the meter; 16,384 GB200 GPUs need about 39 MW. Below roughly 5 MW, colocation is usually fastest. From 5 to 50 MW, energized sites and built halls win. Above that, you are buying a power date, and the date is what you should check first. Invariant finds capacity that fits and checks the power behind it.
takeaways: Start from MW and date, not square feet. Power is the binding constraint for every option.
Dense racks change the shortlist. GB200 NVL72 racks run near 120 kW and need liquid cooling.
A provider’s power date is a risk you inherit. Leases now carry longstop dates for exactly this reason.
Send the GPU count, rack density and date. We send capacity that fits, with the evidence behind each MW figure.

sections.heading: How much power your cluster needs

blocks.text: System power comes from NVIDIA’s own figures: 10.2 kW for an eight-GPU DGX H100, 14.3 kW for an eight-GPU DGX B200, and about 120 kW for a 72-GPU GB200 NVL72 rack. We add about 10% for networking and storage and a PUE of 1.3 for the building.
These are planning figures for sizing a search, not a substitute for your own bill of materials. The full method is in our GPU power guide.

title: How much power does a GPU cluster need? H100, B200 and GB200 NVL72 in MW
description: GPU cluster power requirements in MW: H100, B200 and GB200 NVL72 from 256 to 100,000 GPUs, kW per GPU, rack density, PUE and what to ask a data center for.
intro: A GPU cluster needs about 1.8 kW per H100, 2.6 kW per B200 and 2.4 kW per GB200 GPU at the meter, once you count the server, networking, storage and cooling. That puts 1,024 B200 GPUs at about 2.6 MW, 16,384 GB200 GPUs at about 39 MW and 100,000 GB200 GPUs at about 238 MW. The figures come from NVIDIA’s published system power, plus about 10% for networking and storage and a PUE of 1.3.
takeaways: Size from the system, not the GPU. An H100 is rated up to 700 W, but an eight-GPU DGX H100 draws up to 10.2 kW.
Rack density decides cooling: four DGX H100s is about 41 kW a rack; a GB200 NVL72 is about 120 kW.
PUE turns IT load into what the utility sees. 1.3 is a reasonable planning figure for a new liquid-cooled build.
Ask a data center for MW at the meter and kW per cabinet, both with dates.

columns: kW per GPU, with networking and storage
kW per GPU at the meter (PUE 1.3)
rows: GB200 NVL72 (72 GPUs, about 120 kW a rack)

blocks.text: NVIDIA rates the H100 SXM at up to 700 W, but the GPU is only part of the server. CPUs, memory, NICs and fans take the eight-GPU DGX H100 to 10.2 kW at maximum, and the DGX B200 to 14.3 kW.
The GB200 NVL72 packs 36 Grace CPUs and 72 Blackwell GPUs into one liquid-cooled rack drawing about 120 kW.

Our arithmetic: system kW per GPU, times 1.10 for networking and storage, times 1.3 for PUE. Max-rated system power is a sensible sizing basis because training runs keep GPUs near full load for weeks.

sections.heading: Rack density and what it means for the building

rows: Air with rear-door heat exchangers, or liquid

blocks.text: Most colocation built before 2023 was designed for 5 to 15 kW a cabinet. So the binding question for a dense cluster is often cooling, not floor space or even total MW.

PUE is total facility power divided by IT power. Uptime Institute’s data shows large, newer facilities run more efficiently than the industry average. We use 1.3 for a new liquid-cooled build; an older air-cooled colo hall may run higher, and you pay for that in the power bill or the price per kW.

title: GPU colocation for AI labs and neoclouds: what to ask a provider before you sign
description: GPU colocation checklist for AI labs and neoclouds: power per cabinet, liquid cooling, energized vs contracted MW, delivery dates, minimum terms, fiber and SLAs.
intro: GPU colocation works when a provider can deliver the power per cabinet your racks need, cool it, and do both by your date. Ask for four things in writing: kW per cabinet and the cooling method for your density, total MW energized today versus contracted for later, the delivery date and what it depends on, and the remedy if that date slips. Most halls built before 2023 were designed for 5 to 15 kW a cabinet; a GB200 NVL72 rack runs near 120 kW.
takeaways: Energized MW and contracted MW are different. Ask which one your racks sit on.
Get the cooling method for your exact density, not a general "liquid ready" claim.
A delivery date with no remedy is a hope. Leases with longstop dates exist for this reason.
Check fiber routes and cross-connect pricing early; they shape both latency and cost.

sections.heading: Why the power date is the real risk

blocks.text: Capacity deals fail on dates. Poolside’s planned 2 GW campus deal with CoreWeave broke down over whether the first cluster could be ready in time. Large compute contracts, such as Microsoft’s $9.7 billion deal with IREN, pay against delivery milestones.

Tenants now write power into leases. One data center lease filed with the SEC lets the tenant terminate if firm capacity is not delivered by a longstop date, and gives the tenant approval rights over the power plan.

If you are taking colocation or a lease, you inherit the provider’s power risk. A power check on the provider’s site tells you whether the date is backed by an energized service, a signed agreement, or only a request in a queue.

We find colocation and built capacity that can take your density by your date, and we run a power check on any provider you are already talking to. You get the document behind their MW and what the date depends on, before you sign.

title: Liquid cooling for GPU racks: what a data center needs for 40 to 130 kW racks
description: What a data center needs for liquid-cooled GPU racks: rear-door heat exchangers, direct-to-chip, CDUs, facility water, and how to tell a liquid-ready hall from a real one.
intro: Racks above about 40 kW need liquid somewhere in the cooling path, and racks near 120 kW, like the GB200 NVL72, need direct-to-chip liquid cooling. That means coolant distribution units, a facility water loop sized for the heat, and floor and piping that can carry it. When a provider says "liquid ready", ask what is installed today, at what kW per rack, and what is only planned.
takeaways: Up to about 20 kW a rack, air works in most halls.
About 20 to 50 kW: rear-door heat exchangers or partial liquid.
Above about 50 kW, and for GB200 NVL72 at about 120 kW: direct-to-chip liquid, with CDUs.
"Liquid ready" often means pipes are planned, not installed. Ask for the installed capacity in kW.

rows: Air, hot and cold aisle containment
Chilled or facility water to the rack
CDUs, a facility water loop, leak detection, and air for the remaining heat

blocks.text: NVIDIA designed the GB200 NVL72 as a liquid-cooled rack. There is no air-cooled version to fall back on.

items: How many kW per rack can you cool today, installed, and how many after planned work?
Direct-to-chip or rear-door? Who supplies and maintains the CDUs?
What is the facility water temperature and capacity, and is there redundancy?
How is the remaining air-side heat handled at full density?
Floor loading for a fully populated liquid-cooled rack.
Who owns the risk of a leak, and how is it detected?

blocks.text: Liquid cooling at scale is easier in a new build than a retrofit. That is one reason energized mining sites and new powered shells are attractive for dense clusters: the power is there and the cooling can be built for the racks. Our guide on converting mining sites covers what carries over.

title: Build, lease or colocate: how neoclouds and AI labs get to power fastest
description: Build vs lease vs colocate for neoclouds and AI labs: time to power, capital, control and risk at 5, 50 and 500 MW, and when to move from one to the next.
intro: For a neocloud or AI lab, colocation gets you running fastest with the least capital, leasing a whole building or site gives you control at medium scale, and building on powered land gives the lowest long-run cost per MW but the longest wait and the most risk. The deciding variable is the date power is available, which is why the right choice changes with size: colocation below about 5 MW, a lease from about 5 to 50 MW, and building above that.
takeaways: Time to power usually beats price per kW. Idle GPUs cost far more than rent.
Building means owning the utility relationship, the large-load tariff and its minimum bill.
Leasing moves the power risk to the landlord, but only if the lease says so.
Many neoclouds do all three at once: colo for today, a lease for next year, land for 2028.

rows: Landlord, if the lease says so

blocks.text: Owning the power pays off once the cluster is big and long-lived enough to absorb a long utility term. New large-load tariffs set minimum bills near 80 to 85% of contract demand for 12 years or more, so you need the demand to fill it.
Building also means a utility study cycle. In Texas, large loads now go through ERCOT’s batch process; elsewhere, a load study can take months before construction starts.

Some neoclouds bridge to grid power with on-site gas. It can work, but it has its own clock: turbines, air permits and gas supply. Cleanview counted only about 2 GW running out of some 90 GW of identified behind-the-meter projects.

title: Power longstop dates in GPU and data center leases: check the provider’s power before you sign
description: How AI tenants and neoclouds protect a GPU deployment date: power longstop clauses, what document backs a provider’s MW, and the power check to run before signing.
intro: A power longstop date lets a tenant walk away, or get paid, if the landlord or provider does not deliver firm power by a fixed date. Tenants added these clauses because compute deals keep failing on power dates. Before you rely on one, check the power yourself: which document backs the provider’s MW, which upgrades the date depends on, and whether anyone else is filing for the same capacity. A clause gives you a remedy; only the power check tells you whether you will need it.
takeaways: Longstop clauses are now common in AI data center leases.
Lenders release cash against energization milestones, so a slipped date hits the provider’s financing too.
The document behind the MW is the first thing to check: energized service, signed agreement, load study or nothing.
An independent power study names what the date depends on.

blocks.text: One AI data center lease filed with the SEC lets the tenant terminate if firm capacity is not delivered by a "Firm Capacity Longstop Date", and requires the tenant’s written approval of the power plan: sources, interconnection path, substation and switchgear.

Lenders work the same way. Davis Polk describes power as the risk to settle first in data center financings, and BCLP describes lenders asking for a firm connection date and releasing loan tranches against energization milestones.

Poolside’s planned campus with CoreWeave fell apart over the first cluster’s readiness date. Behind-the-meter plans slip on turbines and air permits; Cleanview counted about 2 GW running out of some 90 GW identified.

Grid dates slip on upgrades, transformer deliveries and utility study cycles. Paces found only about 17% of ERCOT substations near suitable land had any withdrawal headroom, so many dates depend on network upgrades that are not built yet.

sections.heading: The power check to run before signing

items: Get the document behind the MW: energized service, construction agreement, load study, will-serve letter, or a map.
Find the point of interconnection and the utility, and whether the date depends on network upgrades.
Check for other large loads filing at the same substation.
For on-site generation: turbine delivery, air permit status and gas supply.
Run an independent power study on the connection if the date matters to your financing.

blocks.text: Invariant runs this check, usually within 48 hours, and reports what the date depends on in plain terms your counsel and lenders can use.

faqs.question: Can I get an independent check of a data center provider’s power?
faqs.answer: Yes. Invariant checks the document behind the MW, the connection, competing loads, upgrades and on-site generation permits, and runs an N-1 power study where needed, usually within 48 hours.

faqs.question: Who pays for a provider power check?
faqs.answer: Usually the tenant or its lender, before signing or before a draw.

faqs.question: Is this the same as the utility’s study?
faqs.answer: No. The utility’s study commits the utility; ours tells you whether the provider’s date is realistic and what it depends on.

faqs.question: How do I request a power check?
faqs.answer: Email pranav@invariant-ai.com or call (628) 220-8972 with the site or provider, MW and contract date.
